segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was the Mary who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair; it was her brother Lazarus who was sick.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the sisters sent word to him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, look, the one you love is sick.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard it, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This sickness will not end in death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he heard that Lazarus was sick, he then stayed two days in the place where he was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, after this, he said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let us go to Judea again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, just now the Judeans were trying to stone you, and you are going there again?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks during the day, they do not stumble, because they see the light of this world.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if anyone walks at night, they stumble, because the light is not in them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said these things, and after this he told them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will get well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus had been speaking of Lazarus’s death, but they thought he was speaking about ordinary sleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then Jesus told them plainly,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Lazarus has died,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him, but Mary stayed sitting in the house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Your brother will rise again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me will live, even if they die,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After saying this, she went away and called her sister Mary, telling her privately,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still at the place where Martha had met him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary get up quickly and go out, and they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he was stirred to anger in his spirit and deeply troubled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Where have you laid him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, come and see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus wept.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jews said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “See how he loved him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have also kept this one from dying?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus, again stirred to anger within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take away the stone.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, by now he stinks, for it has been four days.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted up his eyes and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I knew that you always hear me, but I said this because of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After saying this, he cried out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Lazarus, come out!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Untie him and let him go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So many of the Jews, those who had come to Mary and seen what he did, believed in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the chief priests and the Pharisees convened a council and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are we doing, when this man is performing many signs?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You know nothing at all,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and you do not consider that it is to your advantage that one man die for the people and the whole nation not perish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not say this on his own; but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So from that day on they planned to kill him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus no longer went about openly among the Jews, but went away from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up to Jerusalem from the countryside before the Passover to purify themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might arrest him.

notes.note: The Greek uses two different verbs for “love” in this chapter: one in verses 3 and 36, another here. Some interpreters find a distinction between a warmer affection and a higher, self-giving love. Most scholars hold that John uses the two interchangeably, since both are applied to the same relationship within a few lines, and the translation renders both “love.”

The Greek word is the one usually translated “Jews,” and it is so translated elsewhere in this chapter. Here the point is geographic: Jesus has proposed returning to Judea, and the disciples recall the hostility he met from people there (10:31). Scholars are divided on how often the word should be rendered “Judeans”; this translation does so only where the regional contrast is in view.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for “save,” which also means to recover from illness. The disciples mean only that sleep is a good sign for a sick man. A reader of this Gospel would likely hear the larger sense as well, one of the unwitting double meanings John often gives to speakers.

notes.traditional: about fifteen furlongs; about two miles
notes.note: A stadion was a Greek measure of roughly 185 meters (about 600 feet). Fifteen stadia is a little under two miles, or about three kilometers, which explains how so many from Jerusalem could come to mourn with the sisters.

The Greek word, traditionally rendered “Christ,” translates the Hebrew title “Messiah,” the anointed king Israel expected. Martha is confessing a title, not using a name, and “Messiah” makes that clear to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

notes.phrase: stirred to anger in his spirit
notes.traditional: groaned in the spirit; deeply moved in spirit
notes.note: Most English versions soften this verb to “deeply moved.” Elsewhere in Greek, and in its other New Testament uses (for example Mark 14:5, where it means to scold), it expresses indignation or stern displeasure, and many commentators accept that sense here. What the anger is directed at is debated: death itself, the unbelief around him, or the scene of grief are all proposed. The same verb recurs in verse 38.

The verb here is not the one used for the weeping of Mary and the mourners in verses 31 and 33, which often describes loud lamentation. This one, found only here in the New Testament, means to shed tears. The contrast may be deliberate: the mourners wail, and Jesus weeps quietly.

notes.traditional: What are we to do?; What do we?
notes.note: The Greek verb is a plain present tense, and the translation keeps it as a self-reproach: nothing is being done while Jesus keeps performing signs. Many versions take it as a deliberative question, “What are we to do?”, which the Greek also allows. The difference in meaning is small.

The Greek word here is the same one that, in the plural, is usually translated “Gentiles,” meaning the non-Jewish peoples. In the singular, as in verses 48 to 52, it means a nation, here the Jewish nation. In verse 50 Caiaphas sets beside it a different word, “people,” the usual term for Israel as God’s people.

“Our place” most likely means the temple, which Jewish writers of the period often called “the place” or “the holy place.” Some take it more broadly as Jerusalem, or as the leaders’ own position. The first readers of this Gospel probably knew that the Romans did destroy the temple in AD 70.

The high priesthood was not an annual office; Caiaphas held it for nearly two decades, from about AD 18 to 36. The phrase, repeated in verse 51, most likely means “in that fateful year,” the year Jesus died. Some scholars have instead taken it as a misunderstanding of the office by the author.

candidates.reason: Occurs in John 11:33, 38 and in Mark 1:43, 14:5 and Matthew 9:30; translations swing between “deeply moved,” “sternly warned” and anger, and the choice should be made once.
The verb covers physical healing, rescue and salvation across the whole New Testament, and a consistent policy is needed for when to render “save” versus “heal” or “recover.”
Translations vary between “council” and “Sanhedrin” throughout the Gospels and Acts, and readers should see one term for the same body.
Ancient units of measure recur in the Gospels and Revelation, and a single policy is needed on keeping the unit versus converting to miles.
Its relation to ἀγαπάω, especially in John 21, needs one decision on whether the two verbs are distinguished in English.
